title: Classic Krusty — The Personality Market

source.notes: Original fan-parody framing and concise paraphrase of the selected personality-market discussion, not a verbatim archival transcript. Fromm voice recreated using a reference from the same 1958 interview.

disclosure: Unofficial fan parody. AI animation and recreated voices. Erich Fromm discussion adapted from his 1958 Mike Wallace interview. Disclosure intended for accompanying post.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Good evening. Our guest tonight is Doctor Erich Fromm, the psychoanalyst and social critic. We will be discussing the personality market: what happens when making a living requires a person to sell more than his work.

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: The problem begins when acceptance matters more than what a person actually is. He starts arranging his character for an audience, asking which version of himself will attract the best offer.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: You distinguish between selling a useful skill and selling the person who possesses it.

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yes. Consider a craftsman. The quality of his work can speak for him. But in many occupations, success also requires a saleable manner: an attractive smile, agreeable opinions, the appearance of confidence. The employee must present himself as a desirable product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And the price becomes a judgment on his worth?

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: That is the danger. If demand falls, he may conclude that there is something wrong with his existence. An unsold object has lost its market value. A human being has not thereby lost his human value. But the marketing outlook makes that distinction difficult to maintain.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So the applause can tell us whether a performance sold. It cannot tell us what the performer is worth.

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: A person needs a basis for self-respect that survives changes in fashion and demand. Otherwise, his sense of himself is always at the mercy of his customers.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Doctor Fromm, thank you for joining us. Our discussion of the individual and the institutions of modern society will continue next week. Good night.
